title: Damayanti in the forest
hook: Damayanti wakes alone in half a cloth, and her dharma is all she has left in the forest
carry: dharma protects the one who protects it

segments.voice: Yesterday: vastra, the one cloth Nala and Damayanti shared, until he cut it in the dark and left. Your line was partners in dharma share the one cloth.

Half a cloth. That's what Damayanti finds when she wakes on the floor of the empty rest house. Half of the garment they shared, and no husband. She calls his name. She runs through the trees calling it, half thinking he's hiding, playing some cruel game. Come out, she says, I'm frightened. Nobody answers. Only the trees, and the empty road, and her own voice coming back. And the story, which has followed Nala until now, turns and follows her.
screen: `HALF A CLOTH.` → `SHE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `THE STORY FOLLOWS HER.`

segments.voice: Her first thought, the story says, is for him: who will look after him now, hungry and alone? Then the forest closes in. A huge serpent seizes her, and even in its coils she cries out for Nala, not for herself. A hunter kills the snake and frees her, then looks at her the wrong way. Damayanti has nothing left: no husband, no kingdom, half a cloth. But she still has her faithfulness, and she calls on it. The hunter falls dead. She walks on and asks everything she meets. A mountain. Ascetics, who promise she'll see Nala again and then vanish, hermitage and all. An Ashoka tree in bloom, whose name means without sorrow: live up to your name, she begs it, and take mine. At last she reaches the city of Chedi, ragged, and the queen mother takes her in. Even as a servant, she sets her own terms and keeps them. Now the teaching. There's a Sanskrit line many Hindus know by heart: dharmo rakshati rakshitah. Dharma protects the one who protects it. Dharma is what's right for you to do: your duty, your faithfulness, your truth. Many teachers read Damayanti's road as that line told as a story. Everything a person can lose, she lost. What she wouldn't give up was her dharma, and in the forest, it kept her. Notice what the line doesn't promise. Her road was terrible. It promises that the one thing you guard will guard you back. For today: the line matters most when keeping what's right costs you something, and no one would ever know.
screen: `THE SERPENT AND THE HUNTER.` · `"ASHOKA, TAKE MY SORROW."` · `DHARMO RAKSHATI RAKSHITAH.` · then, large: `DHARMA PROTECTS THE ONE WHO PROTECTS IT.`

segments.voice: Damayanti had nothing to hold but her dharma. Bring to mind one right thing you're keeping right now, a promise, an honesty, a kindness no one sees, and rest with it as you breathe. If you pray, say dharmo rakshati rakshitah softly and ask for strength to keep guarding it; if not, simply notice what it would cost to let it go, and what it gives you to keep it.
Ashoka, the tree whose name means without sorrow. Damayanti asked it to take hers, and walked on with her dharma whole.
Your line: dharma protects the one who protects it. Damayanti kept hers, and it kept her. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Damayanti's wandering, from the forest to the court of Chedi, is told in the Nala story of the Mahabharata's Vana Parva; many teachers read it alongside the well-known line dharmo rakshati rakshitah, dharma protects the one who protects it.
